messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Let's add a new feature—bots. Bots can be members of rooms and post messages via an HTTP API.

Any chat member can create and manage bots via the user interface:
- open the account settings page (`/account/edit`)
- click the bot icon ("Set up chat bots")

This opens the bots page (`/bots`). It lists the bots you created (administrators see all bots) and has the "Add a chat bot" button. The button opens the `/bots/new` page with a form:

- bot avatar (optional)
- bot name (required), labelled "Name the bot"
- the "Save changes" button

Submitting the form creates a bot and redirects back to `/bots`. Each bot on the list shows its name and its unique bot code in a read-only field labelled "Bot code", in the same list item—the code is used to authenticate bot requests. The bot code is a sensitive credential. The bots page shows all of your bots on one page, without pagination.

From the list, you can also edit a bot (name, avatar): each bot has an "Edit <bot name>" link (for example, "Edit Deploy Bot") to its edit page. The edit page uses the same form and has a "Delete this chat bot" button that asks for confirmation. A deleted bot can no longer post messages.

Like any new user, a new bot joins all open rooms. Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people.

Here is how a bot can post a message:

```
curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \
  https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages
```

Bots can post from shell scripts and CI jobs. The raw request body becomes the message body. No JSON envelope, no field names.

The endpoint responds with:

- `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`
- `422 Unprocessable Content` — empty body and no attachment
- `404 Not Found` — bad room id
- `401 Unauthorized` — invalid bot code

The message is broadcast to connected clients and triggers push notifications exactly as a human-authored message would.

The message shows the bot (its name) as the author.

# Campfire

Campfire is a web-based chat application. It supports many of the features you'd
expect, including:

- Multiple rooms, with access controls
- Direct messages
- File attachments with previews
- Search
- Notifications (via Web Push)
- @mentions

## Running your own Campfire instance

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional,
single-machine deployment. This includes the web app, background jobs, caching,
file serving, and SSL. You can use our pre-built image at
`ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, or build your own from this repo.

### Deploying with ONCE

The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).
It will guide you through the initial set up and then keep your instance up to date automatically.

If you don't already have `once` installed, run this on the machine you want to run Campfire on:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com | sh
```

`once` will launch as soon as the install is finished. 

Choose Campfire from the list of applications, follow the instructions, and ONCE will take care of the rest.

If you prefer the command line to the dashboard, you can deploy directly:

```sh
once deploy ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire --host chat.example.com
```

### Deploying with Docker

If you'd rather run the Docker image yourself, you can read more about that in the [self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md).

> [!TIP]
> When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through a wizard to create an admin account.
> The email address that you enter for the admin account will be visible on the sign-in page, it's there so
> that people have someone to contact if they need help with their account. If that bothers you, put in any
> email address you want and create yourself a new admin account.

## Development

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
Please see our [development guide](docs/development.md) for how to get Campfire set up for local development.

## Security

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for how to report a vulnerability and a description of our trust model.
# How to contribute to Campfire

Campfire uses GitHub
[discussions](https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/discussions) to track
feature requests and questions, rather than [the issue
tracker](https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/issues). If you're considering
opening an issue or pull request, please open a discussion instead.

Whenever a discussion leads to an actionable and well-understood task, we'll
move it to the issue tracker where it can be worked on.

This is a little different than how some other projects work, but it makes it
easier for us to triage and prioritise the work. It also means that the open
issues all represent agreed-upon tasks that are either being worked on, or are
ready to be worked on.

This should also make it easier to see what's in progress, and to find
something to work on if you'd like to do so.

## What this means in practice

### If you'd like to contribute to the code...

1. If you're interested in working on one of the open issues, please do! We are
   grateful for the help!
2. You'll want to make sure someone else isn't already working on the same
   issue. If they are, it will be tagged "in progress" and/or it should be clear
   from the comments. When in doubt, you can always comment on the issue to ask.
3. Similarly, if you need any help or guidance on the issue, please comment on
   the issue as you go, and we'll do our best to help.
4. When you have something ready for review or collaboration, open a PR.

### If you've found a bug...

1. If you don't have steps to reproduce the problem, or you're not certain it's a
   bug, open a discussion.
2. If you have steps to reproduce, open an issue.

### If you have an idea for a feature...

1. Open a discussion.

### If you have a question, or are having trouble with configuration...

1. Open a discussion.

Hopefully this process makes it easier for everyone to be involved. Thanks for
helping! ❤️

module Membership::Connectable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  CONNECTION_TTL = 60.seconds

  included do
    scope :connected,    -> { where(connected_at: CONNECTION_TTL.ago..) }
    scope :disconnected, -> { where(connected_at: [ nil, ...CONNECTION_TTL.ago ]) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def disconnect_all
      connected.update_all connected_at: nil, connections: 0, updated_at: Time.current
    end

    def connect(membership, connections)
      where(id: membership.id).update_all(connections: connections, connected_at: Time.current, unread_at: nil)
    end
  end

  def connected?
    connected_at? && connected_at >= CONNECTION_TTL.ago
  end

  def present
    self.class.connect(self, connected? ? connections + 1 : 1)
  end

  def connected
    increment_connections
    touch :connected_at
  end

  def disconnected
    decrement_connections
    update! connected_at: nil if connections < 1
  end

  def refresh_connection
    increment_connections unless connected?
    touch :connected_at
  end

  def increment_connections
    connected? ? increment!(:connections, touch: true) : update!(connections: 1)
  end

  def decrement_connections
    connected? ? decrement!(:connections, touch: true) : update!(connections: 0)
  end
end

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.insert_all(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end
end

  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload

        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)

      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_mentions).where(user_id: mentionees.ids)

      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

    def enqueue_payload_for_delivery(payload, subscriptions)
      Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.queue(payload, subscriptions)

  after_create_commit -> { room.receive(self) }

  scope :ordered, -> { order(:created_at) }
  scope :with_creator, -> { preload(creator: :avatar_attachment) }
  scope :with_attachment_details, -> {
    with_rich_text_body_and_embeds
    with_attached_attachment
      .includes(attachment_blob: :variant_records)
  }
  scope :with_boosts, -> { includes(boosts: :booster) }

  def plain_text_body
    body.to_plain_text.presence || attachment&.filename&.to_s || ""
  end

  def to_key
    [ client_message_id ]
  end

  def content_type
    case
    when attachment?    then "attachment"
    when sound.present? then "sound"
    else                     "text"
    end.inquiry
  end

  def sound
    plain_text_body.match(/\A\/play (?<name>\w+)\z/) do |match|
      Sound.find_by_name match[:name]
    end
  end
end

module Message::Broadcasts
  def broadcast_create
    broadcast_append_to room, :messages, target: [ room, :messages ]
    broadcast_unread_room
  end

  def broadcast_remove
    broadcast_remove_to room, :messages
  end

  private
    # Fanned out to the room's members rather than published on one global stream, so
    # that the timing of activity in a room only reaches people who are in it.
    def broadcast_unread_room
      room.memberships.pluck(:user_id).each do |user_id|
        ActionCable.server.broadcast UnreadRoomsChannel.stream_name_for(user_id), { roomId: room.id }
      end
    end
end

    end

    def create_with_attachment!(attributes)
      create!(attributes).tap(&:process_attachment)
    end

    attachment.attached?

    ensure_attachment_analyzed
    process_attachment_thumbnail
  end

class RoomsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_room, only: %i[ show destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ destroy ]
  before_action :remember_last_room_visited, only: :show

  def index
    redirect_to room_url(Current.user.rooms.last)
  end

  def show
    @messages = find_messages
  end

  def destroy
    @room.destroy

    broadcast_remove_room
    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def set_room
      if room = room_scope.find_by(id: params[:room_id] || params[:id])
        @room = room
      else
        redirect_to root_url, alert: "Room not found or inaccessible"
      end
    end

    # Subclasses narrow this to the room types they're allowed to act on, so that one
    # room namespace can't be used to reach another's rooms.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@room)
    end

    def ensure_permission_to_create_rooms
      if Current.account.settings.restrict_room_creation_to_administrators? && !Current.user.administrator?
        head :forbidden
      end
    end

    def find_messages
      messages = @room.messages.with_creator.with_attachment_details.with_boosts

      if show_first_message = messages.find_by(id: params[:message_id])
        @messages = messages.page_around(show_first_message)
      else
        @messages = messages.last_page
      end
    end

    def room_params
      params.require(:room).permit(:name)
    end

    def broadcast_remove_room
      broadcast_remove_to :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ]
    end
end

  before_action :set_room, only: %i[ show edit update ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ update ]
  before_action :remember_last_room_visited, only: :show
  before_action :force_room_type, only: %i[ edit update ]
  before_action :ensure_permission_to_create_rooms, only: %i[ new create ]

  DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME = "New room"

  def show
    redirect_to room_url(@room)
  end

  def new
    @room  = Rooms::Closed.new(name: DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME)
    @users = User.active.ordered
  end

  def create
    room = Rooms::Closed.create_for(room_params, users: grantees)

    broadcast_create_room(room)
    redirect_to room_url(room)
  end

  def edit
    selected_user_ids = @room.users.pluck(:id)
    @selected_users, @unselected_users = User.active.ordered.partition { |user| selected_user_ids.include?(user.id) }
  end

  def update
    @room.update! room_params
    @room.memberships.revise(granted: grantees, revoked: revokees)

    broadcast_update_room
    redirect_to room_url(@room)
  end

  private
    # Allows us to edit an open room and turn it into a closed one on saving.
    def force_room_type
      @room = @room.becomes!(Rooms::Closed)
    end

    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other, so both are in reach here. Direct
    # rooms never are: converting one would let its creator revise who's in it.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms.without_directs
    end

    def grantees
      User.where(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def revokees
      @room.users.where.not(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def grantee_ids
      params.fetch(:user_ids, [])
    end

    def broadcast_create_room(room)
      each_user_and_html_for(room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_prepend_to user, :rooms, target: :shared_rooms, html: html
      end
    end

    def broadcast_update_room
      each_user_and_html_for(@room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_replace_to user, :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ], html: html
      end
    end

    def each_user_and_html_for(room)
      # Optimization to avoid rendering the same partial for every user
      html = render_to_string(partial: "users/sidebars/rooms/shared", locals: { room: room })

      room.users.each { |user| yield user, html }
    end
end

  before_action :ensure_permission_to_create_rooms, only: %i[ new create ]

  DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME = "New room"

  def show
    redirect_to room_url(@room)
  end

  def new
    @room  = Rooms::Closed.new(name: DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME)
    @users = User.active.ordered
  end

  def create
    room = Rooms::Closed.create_for(room_params, users: grantees)

    broadcast_create_room(room)
    redirect_to room_url(room)
  end

  def edit
    selected_user_ids = @room.users.pluck(:id)
    @selected_users, @unselected_users = User.active.ordered.partition { |user| selected_user_ids.include?(user.id) }
  end

  def update
    @room.update! room_params
    @room.memberships.revise(granted: grantees, revoked: revokees)

    broadcast_update_room
    redirect_to room_url(@room)
  end

  private
    # Allows us to edit an open room and turn it into a closed one on saving.
    def force_room_type
      @room = @room.becomes!(Rooms::Closed)
    end

    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other, so both are in reach here. Direct
    # rooms never are: converting one would let its creator revise who's in it.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms.without_directs
    end

    def grantees
      User.where(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def revokees
      @room.users.where.not(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def grantee_ids
      params.fetch(:user_ids, [])
    end

    def broadcast_create_room(room)
      each_user_and_html_for(room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_prepend_to user, :rooms, target: :shared_rooms, html: html
      end
    end

    def broadcast_update_room
      each_user_and_html_for(@room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_replace_to user, :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ], html: html
      end
    end

    def each_user_and_html_for(room)
      # Optimization to avoid rendering the same partial for every user
      html = render_to_string(partial: "users/sidebars/rooms/shared", locals: { room: room })

      room.users.each { |user| yield user, html }
    end
end

module ApplicationHelper
  def page_title_tag
    tag.title @page_title || "Campfire"
  end

  def current_user_meta_tags
    unless Current.user.nil?
      safe_join [
        tag(:meta, name: "current-user-id", content: Current.user.id),
        tag(:meta, name: "current-user-name", content: Current.user.name)
      ]
    end
  end

  def custom_styles_tag
    if custom_styles = Current.account&.custom_styles
      tag.style(custom_styles.to_s.html_safe, data: { turbo_track: "reload" })
    end
  end

  def body_classes
    [ @body_class, admin_body_class, account_logo_body_class ].compact.join(" ")
  end

  def link_back
    back_url = request.referrer
    back_url = root_path if back_url.nil? || back_url == request.url
    link_back_to back_url
  end

  def link_back_to(destination)
    link_to destination, class: "btn" do
      image_tag("arrow-left.svg", aria: { hidden: "true" }, size: 20) +
      tag.span("Go Back", class: "for-screen-reader")
    end
  end

  private
    def admin_body_class
      "admin" if Current.user&.can_administer?
    end

    def account_logo_body_class
      "account-has-logo" if Current.account&.logo&.attached?
    end
end

module ApplicationHelper
  def page_title_tag
    tag.title @page_title || "Campfire"
  end

  def current_user_meta_tags
    unless Current.user.nil?
      safe_join [
        tag(:meta, name: "current-user-id", content: Current.user.id),
        tag(:meta, name: "current-user-name", content: Current.user.name)
      ]
    end
  end

  def custom_styles_tag
    if custom_styles = Current.account&.custom_styles
      tag.style(custom_styles.to_s.html_safe, data: { turbo_track: "reload" })
    end
  end

  def body_classes
    [ @body_class, admin_body_class, account_logo_body_class ].compact.join(" ")
  end

  def link_back
    back_url = request.referrer
    back_url = root_path if back_url.nil? || back_url == request.url
    link_back_to back_url
  end

  def link_back_to(destination)
    link_to destination, class: "btn" do
      image_tag("arrow-left.svg", aria: { hidden: "true" }, size: 20) +
      tag.span("Go Back", class: "for-screen-reader")
    end
  end

  private
    def admin_body_class
      "admin" if Current.user&.can_administer?
    end

    def account_logo_body_class
      "account-has-logo" if Current.account&.logo&.attached?
    end
end

class ContentFilters::RemoveSoloUnfurledLinkText < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    normalize_tweet_url(solo_unfurled_url) == normalize_tweet_url(content.to_plain_text)
  end

  def apply
    fragment.replace("div") { |node| node.tap { |n| n.inner_html = unfurled_links.first.to_s } }
  end

  private
    TWITTER_DOMAINS = %w[ x.com twitter.com ]
    TWITTER_DOMAIN_MAPPING = { "x.com" => "twitter.com" }

    def solo_unfurled_url
      unfurled_links.first["href"] if unfurled_links.size == 1
    end

    def unfurled_links
      fragment.find_all("action-text-attachment[@content-type='#{ActionText::Attachment::OpengraphEmbed::OPENGRAPH_EMBED_CONTENT_TYPE}']")
    end

    def normalize_tweet_url(url)
      return url unless twitter_url?(url)

      uri = URI.parse(url)

      uri.dup.tap do |u|
        u.host = TWITTER_DOMAIN_MAPPING[uri.host&.downcase] || uri.host
        u.query = nil
      end.to_s
    rescue URI::InvalidURIError
      url
    end

    def twitter_url?(url)
      url.present? && TWITTER_DOMAINS.any? { |domain| url.strip.include?(domain) }
    end
end
class ContentFilters::SanitizeAttributes < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    true
  end

  # Scrub attributes on the tags that SanitizeTags allows, using Rails' safe-list
  # sanitizer so unsafe URI schemes and event-handler attributes are stripped.
  # Runs after SanitizeTags, so passing the same allowed tags makes the tag pass
  # a no-op and only attributes are scrubbed.
  def apply
    sanitizer.sanitize fragment.to_html, tags: allowed_tags, attributes: allowed_attributes
  end

  private
    # Presentation styling relies on class attributes (e.g. unfurled link embeds),
    # which the standard ActionText set doesn't include.
    EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES = %w[ class ]

    # ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer is a single process-wide instance, and
    # rails-html-sanitizer reuses one mutable permit scrubber that it reconfigures
    # from the tags/attributes on every #sanitize call. Sharing it here would race
    # our stricter tag set against ActionText's default rendering on concurrent
    # requests, so use a dedicated instance of the same sanitizer class to keep the
    # scrubber isolated.
    def sanitizer
      sanitizer_class.new
    end

    def sanitizer_class
      ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer.class
    end

    def allowed_tags
      ContentFilters::SanitizeTags::ALLOWED_TAGS
    end

    def allowed_attributes
      standard_allowed_attributes + EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES
    end

    # Mirrors ActionText::ContentHelper#sanitizer_allowed_attributes, which isn't
    # exposed at the module level.
    def standard_allowed_attributes
      ActionText::ContentHelper.allowed_attributes ||
        (sanitizer_class.allowed_attributes + ActionText::Attachment::ATTRIBUTES).to_a
    end
end
class ContentFilters::SanitizeTags < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    true
  end

  def apply
    fragment.replace(not_allowed_tags_css_selector) { nil }
  end

  private
    ALLOWED_TAGS = %w[ a abbr acronym address b big blockquote br cite code dd del dfn div dl dt em h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 h6 hr i ins kbd li ol
      p pre samp small span strong sub sup time tt ul var ] + [ ActionText::Attachment.tag_name, "figure", "figcaption" ]

    def not_allowed_tags_css_selector
      ALLOWED_TAGS.map { |tag| ":not(#{tag})" }.join("")
    end
end
class ContentFilters::StyleUnfurledTwitterAvatars < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    unfurled_twitter_avatars.present?
  end

  def apply
    fragment.update do |source|
      div = source.at_css("div")
      div["class"] = UNFURLED_TWITTER_AVATAR_CSS_CLASS
    end
  end

  private
    UNFURLED_TWITTER_AVATAR_CSS_CLASS = "cf-twitter-avatar"
    TWITTER_AVATAR_URL_PREFIX = "https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images"

    def unfurled_twitter_avatars
      fragment.find_all("#{opengraph_css_selector}[url*='#{TWITTER_AVATAR_URL_PREFIX}']")
    end

    def opengraph_css_selector
      "action-text-attachment[@content-type='#{ActionText::Attachment::OpengraphEmbed::OPENGRAPH_EMBED_CONTENT_TYPE}']"
    end
end

module TurboTestHelper
  def assert_rendered_turbo_stream_broadcast(*streambles, action:, target:, &block)
    streams = find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
    target = ActionView::RecordIdentifier.dom_id(*target)
    assert_select Nokogiri::HTML.fragment(streams), %(turbo-stream[action="#{action}"][target="#{target}"]), &block
  end

  private
    def find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
      broadcasting = streambles.collect do |streamble|
        streamble.try(:to_gid_param) || streamble
      end.join(":")

      broadcasts.collect { |b| JSON.parse(b) }.join("\n\n")

module TurboTestHelper
  def assert_rendered_turbo_stream_broadcast(*streambles, action:, target:, &block)
    streams = find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
    target = ActionView::RecordIdentifier.dom_id(*target)
    assert_select Nokogiri::HTML.fragment(streams), %(turbo-stream[action="#{action}"][target="#{target}"]), &block
  end

  private
    def find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
      broadcasting = streambles.collect do |streamble|
        streamble.try(:to_gid_param) || streamble
      end.join(":")

      broadcasts = ActionCable.server.pubsub.broadcasts(broadcasting)
      broadcasts.collect { |b| JSON.parse(b) }.join("\n\n")
    end
end
module NetworkTestHelper
  # URL validation resolves hostnames through real DNS (see RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard),
  # which WebMock can't intercept. Checked once at boot so per-test Resolv stubs don't interfere.
  DNS_AVAILABLE = begin
    Resolv.getaddresses("example.com").any?
  rescue StandardError
    false
  end

  # Skip tests that depend on DNS resolution when running in an offline sandbox
  # (e.g., a Docker container with no outside network access).
  def skip_unless_dns
    skip "DNS resolution is unavailable (offline sandbox)" unless DNS_AVAILABLE
  end

require "surfguard"

module RestrictedHTTP
  class Violation < StandardError; end

  # The address policy lives in the surfguard gem so this app, Basecamp, HEY and
  # Fizzy classify "internal" the same way instead of each keeping a copy that
  # drifts. The callers here hand a bare hostname in and pin the address that
  # comes back, so this stays a hostname-in, address-out shim.
  module PrivateNetworkGuard
    extend self

    # A hostname that resolves to nothing (NXDOMAIN, timeout, empty answer)
    # raises Surfguard::Unresolvable, which we let propagate as a lookup failure
    # -- the same way the old Resolv.getaddress guard raised Resolv::ResolvError,
    # and the callers here already treat it as a fetch failure. The Violation is
    # reserved for a host that resolves to a blocked address (an empty list back
    # from resolve_public_ips), so a transient DNS miss is never misreported as
    # an SSRF attempt.
    def resolve(hostname)
      Surfguard.resolve_public_ips(hostname).first or
        raise Violation.new("Attempt to access private IP via #{hostname}")
    end

    def private_ip?(ip)
      Surfguard.blocked_address?(ip)
    end
  end
end

      response = http.request uri, req
    else
      resp = http.request(req)

require_relative 'constants'

module Rack
  class MethodOverride
    HTTP_METHODS = %w[GET HEAD PUT POST DELETE OPTIONS PATCH LINK UNLINK]

    METHOD_OVERRIDE_PARAM_KEY = "_method"
    HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE_HEADER = "HTTP_X_HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE"

    def initialize(app)

    def call(env)

        method = method_override(env)
        if HTTP_METHODS.include?(method)

          env[REQUEST_METHOD] = method

require_relative 'constants'
require_relative 'request'
require_relative 'utils'

module Rack
  class MethodOverride
    HTTP_METHODS = %w[GET HEAD PUT POST DELETE OPTIONS PATCH LINK UNLINK]

    METHOD_OVERRIDE_PARAM_KEY = "_method"
    HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE_HEADER = "HTTP_X_HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE"
    ALLOWED_METHODS = %w[POST]

    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    def call(env)
      if allowed_methods.include?(env[REQUEST_METHOD])
        method = method_override(env)
        if HTTP_METHODS.include?(method)
          env[RACK_METHODOVERRIDE_ORIGINAL_METHOD] = env[REQUEST_METHOD]
          env[REQUEST_METHOD] = method
        end
      end

      @app.call(env)
    end

    def method_override(env)
      req = Request.new(env)
      method = method_override_param(req) ||
        env[HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE_HEADER]
      begin
        method.to_s.upcase
      rescue ArgumentError
        env[RACK_ERRORS].puts "Invalid string for method"
      end
    end

    private

    def allowed_methods
      ALLOWED_METHODS
    end

    def method_override_param(req)
      req.POST[METHOD_OVERRIDE_PARAM_KEY] if req.form_data? || req.parseable_data?
    rescue Utils::InvalidParameterError, Utils::ParameterTypeError, QueryParser::ParamsTooDeepError
      req.get_header(RACK_ERRORS).puts "Invalid or incomplete POST params"
    rescue EOFError
      req.get_header(RACK_ERRORS).puts "Bad request content body"
    end

## Development

### Setting up

First, get everything installed and configured with:

```sh
bin/setup
```

This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally).

If you want to start over at any point, run:

```sh
bin/setup --reset
```

### Running the server

Start the development server with:

```sh
bin/dev
```

You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000.

On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on.

Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back.

### Web Push notifications

Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables:

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`

You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running:

```sh
script/admin/generate-secrets
```

### Running tests

Run the unit tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test
```

And the browser-based system tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test:system
```

Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command:

```sh
bin/ci
```

### Contributing

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first.

messages.content:
`request_parameters=` is public, so the endpoint can opt out of body parsing cleanly. I have enough context to design this, so here's the plan before I write code.

**Design**
- **Bot = Bot record + its own `User`.** Messages, memberships, avatars and push all key off `User`, so a bot behaves like any other member. The `bots` table holds the `code` credential and `creator` (the owner), keeping the credential out of `users`.
- **Creator-based permissions.** `User#can_administer?(record)` already checks `record.creator`, so owners and admins can manage bots without new authorization code.
- **Bot API** at `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` takes the raw body as plain text. It skips form and JSON parsing and CSRF, escapes the text before storing it as rich text, and returns 401/404/422/201 as specified.
- **Credential hygiene.** Mask the bot code in request logs, parameter logs and Sentry URLs.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > app/models/bot.rb <<'EOF'
# Bots post into rooms over HTTP, authenticating with their code. Each bot acts through its own user, so
# its messages, memberships and notifications work exactly as they do for people. The code is the bot's
# credential: whoever holds it can post as the bot, so it's only shown to the bot's creator and admins.
class Bot < ApplicationRecord
  has_secure_token :code

  belongs_to :user, autosave: true
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validates :name, presence: true

  delegate :name, to: :user, allow_nil: true

  scope :ordered, -> { joins(:user).order("LOWER(users.name)") }

  class << self
    # Deactivating a bot's user destroys the bot, but a user can also be banned, so only active users' bots can
    # authenticate.
    def authenticate(code)
      joins(:user).merge(User.active).find_by(code: code) if code.present?
    end
  end

  def name=(name)
    bot_user.name = name
  end

  def avatar=(avatar)
    bot_user.avatar = avatar
  end

  private
    # Bots never sign in, so the random password only satisfies the user's password digest.
    def bot_user
      user || build_user(password: SecureRandom.hex)
    end
end
EOF

class BotsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_bot, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]

  def index
    @bots = visible_bots.ordered.preload(:creator, user: :avatar_attachment)
  end

  def new
    @bot = Bot.new
  end

  def create
    @bot = Bot.new(bot_params)

    if @bot.save
      redirect_to bots_url
    else
      render :new, status: :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  def edit
  end

  def update
    if @bot.update(bot_params)
      redirect_to bots_url
    else
      render :edit, status: :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  def destroy
    @bot.user.deactivate

    redirect_to bots_url
  end

  private
    def set_bot
      @bot = Bot.find(params[:id])
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@bot)
    end

    # Administrators manage every bot; everyone else only the bots they created.
    def visible_bots
      Current.user.can_administer? ? Bot.all : Current.user.bots
    end

    # A file field submits nil when no file is chosen, which would otherwise remove the current avatar.
    def bot_params
      params.require(:bot).permit(:name, :avatar).compact
    end
end

messages.content: `raw_post` goes through `read_body_stream`, so it handles chunked bodies too, and `request_parameters` aliases `POST`. Next I'll write the bot message controller.

arguments.command:
cd /app && mkdir -p app/controllers/bots && cat > app/controllers/bots/messages_controller.rb <<'EOF' # Lets bots post messages from scripts and CI jobs. The bot code in the path is the only credential, and the # raw request body is the message: no JSON envelope, no field names. Multipart uploads are the one exception, # carrying an optional `attachment` file and an optional `body` text field. class Bots::MessagesController < ApplicationController include ActiveStorage::SetCurrent allow_unauthenticated_access skip_forgery_protection before_action :set_bot, :set_room, :ensure_content_present def create message = @room.messages.create_with_attachment!(message_attributes) message.broadcast_create head :created, location: message_path(message) end private # The body is the message, not parameters. Left alone, Rails would parse it as a form or JSON document # before any action runs, and a body such as "100% done" would be rejected with a 400. Multipart is the # exception, since its attachment has to be parsed. def process_action(*) request.request_parameters = {} unless multipart? super end def set_bot @bot = Bot.authenticate(params[:bot_code]) head :unauthorized unless @bot end def set_room @room = @bot.user.rooms.find_by(id: params[:room_id]) head :not_found unless @room end def ensure_content_present head :unprocessable_content if message_text.blank? && uploaded_attachment.nil? end def message_attributes { creator: @bot.user, body: (message_html if message_text.present?), attachment: uploaded_attachment }.compact end # Bot text is plain text, so it's escaped before being stored as rich text: markup in it is shown as written. def message_html ERB::Util.html_escape(message_text).gsub("\n", "
") end def message_text @message_text ||= read_text.gsub(/\r\n?/, "\n").strip end def read_text if multipart? params[:body].to_s else request.raw_post.dup.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8).scrub end end def uploaded_attachment params[:attachment] if multipart? && params[:attachment].is_a?(ActionDispatch::Http::UploadedFile) end def multipart? request.media_type == "multipart/form-data" end end EOF echo ok

messages.content: The account page nav is updated. Next are the credential-hygiene pieces: a `BotCodeFilter` that masks codes in paths and URLs, a Rails path-filter hook so request logs mask them, the `:bot_code` parameter filter, and a Sentry `before_send` hook.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > lib/bot_code_filter.rb <<'EOF'
# Bot codes are credentials carried in the path of every bot message (POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages),
# so anything that records request paths or URLs has to mask them.
module BotCodeFilter
  MASK = "[FILTERED]"
  PATTERN = %r{(/rooms/[^/?#]+/)[^/?#]+(/messages\b)}

  def self.filter(path_or_url)
    path_or_url.to_s.gsub(PATTERN, "\\1#{MASK}\\2")
  end
end
EOF
cat > lib/rails_ext/request_filtered_path.rb <<'EOF'
# Rails logs request.filtered_path, which only masks query parameters. Bot codes sit in the path, so mask them here too.
module BotCodeFilteredPath
  def filtered_path
    BotCodeFilter.filter(super)
  end
end

ActionDispatch::Request.prepend BotCodeFilteredPath
EOF

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > docs/bots.md <<'EOF' # Chat bots Bots are chat members that post messages over HTTP. They're aimed at shell scripts and CI jobs: a deploy script can announce that it finished, a test run can post its summary. ## Model - `Bot` (`bots` table) holds the bot's **code**, the credential that authenticates its requests, and its **creator** (the person who set it up). - Each bot has its own `User` (`bots.user_id`, one-to-one). That user carries the bot's name and avatar and is what messages, memberships and notifications point at. So a bot is an ordinary member as far as the rest of the app is concerned: it's named and avatared like anyone, shows as the author of its messages, joins open rooms when it's created, can be granted closed rooms like anyone, and triggers push notifications the same way. - The bot's user has no email address and a random password nobody knows. Bots never sign in, but the users table requires a password digest. - Deleting a bot (`User#deactivate`, which the bot's delete button and the account members list both use) deactivates its user, the same as for people, and destroys the `Bot` row. That removes the code, so the bot can't post, but its past messages stay attributed to it. Permissions reuse `User#can_administer?(record)`, which already lets a record's creator or an administrator manage it. Any member can create bots. The list shows your own bots, or every bot for administrators. ## Web UI - `/account/edit` has a bot icon link ("Set up chat bots") for every member, not only administrators. - `/bots` lists the bots (no pagination). Each item shows the name, the creator (for administrators), an edit link ("Edit "), and a read-only "Bot code" field with a copy button. The page is marked `turbo-cache-control: no-cache` so Turbo doesn't keep codes in its page cache. - `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` share one form: avatar (optional), name ("Name the bot", required), "Save changes". The edit page adds "Delete this chat bot", which asks for confirmation with Turbo's `data-turbo-confirm` (the native `confirm()`). - Forms that fail validation re-render with status 422. - An empty file field doesn't clear the current avatar. The controller drops blank `avatar` params. ## HTTP API ``` curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \ https://chat.example.com/rooms///messages ``` Route: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` (`bot_messages_path`), handled by `Bots::MessagesController`. | Situation | Status | |---------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------| | Message created | `201 Created`, `Location: /messages/:id` | | Unknown, deleted or banned bot code | `401 Unauthorized` | | Room doesn't exist, or the bot isn't a member of it | `404 Not Found` | | Empty or whitespace-only body and no attachment | `422 Unprocessable Content` | Checks run in that order, so an unknown code gets 401 whatever the room is. A response never includes the code. Request bodies: - **Any content type is taken as plain text.** The raw body is the message, with no JSON envelope and no field names. A body such as `100% done`, `a=b&c=d` or `{not json` is posted as written. Rails never parses it (see below). - The text is trimmed, and line breaks (`\r\n` or `\n`) are kept as line breaks. - Invalid UTF-8 bytes are replaced with U+FFFD. - **Multipart** (`curl -F`) is the one exception: an `attachment` file becomes the message's attachment, and an optional `body` field supplies text. A multipart request with neither is a 422. Message content: the text is HTML-escaped before it's stored as rich text, so markup in it is shown literally, and URLs still autolink like anywhere else. Newlines are stored as `
` so they show up in the message. Once created, the message goes through the same path as a person's: it's broadcast to the room (`Message#broadcast_create`), marks the room unread for members, and enqueues `Room::PushMessageJob`. ## Security notes - **The code is a credential.** It's 24 random base58 characters (`has_secure_token`), unique, and stored as-is, because the list has to show it. Anyone who holds it can post as the bot, so: - It's only shown to the bot's creator and to administrators, on `/bots`. Edit and delete pages don't show it. - It travels in the URL path, which is why it's masked everywhere a path or URL gets recorded: - Request logs: `lib/rails_ext/request_filtered_path.rb` prepends to `ActionDispatch::Request#filtered_path`, and `BotCodeFilter` masks `/rooms/:id//messages`. Parameter logs mask `code` (`filter_parameter_logging.rb`). - Sentry: `config/initializers/sentry.rb` scrubs the request URL in `before_send`. - Deactivating a user, or banning one, stops its bots from authenticating (`Bot.authenticate` only accepts active users). - The endpoint is outside the session and CSRF machinery: `allow_unauthenticated_access`, `skip_forgery_protection`. - Rails' parameter parsing is skipped for the body (`Bots::MessagesController#process_action`). Otherwise Rails parses form bodies (`100% done` is an invalid form, so it gets a 400) and JSON bodies (malformed JSON gets a 400). Multipart requests are still parsed, for the attachment. - Bot text is HTML-escaped before it's stored, so bots can't inject markup into other people's pages. ## Known limits and follow-ups - The code isn't encrypted at rest. The app doesn't configure Active Record encryption keys, and the code has to be shown on the list. Adding encryption would mean adding keys to deployments, and `find_by(code:)` would need deterministic encryption. - There's no way to rotate a code yet. Deleting and recreating the bot is the workaround. A "Regenerate code" action is the natural next step. - No rate limiting on the bot endpoint. A leaked code can flood a room until its bot is deleted. - SQL debug logs show the literal values SQLite queries use, including bot codes and session tokens, so don't run production at `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. - Bot-authored messages don't show a "bot" badge. The author name is the only marker. - No attachment size limit beyond what's already in place for people. - System tests need a chromedriver. They didn't run in the sandbox this was built in (it has no network to download one), so the UI was checked with controller tests and by driving the running app over HTTP. EOF wc -l docs/bots.md

# Bots post into rooms over HTTP, authenticating with their code. Each bot acts through its own user, so its
# messages, memberships and notifications work exactly as they do for people. The code is the bot's credential:
# whoever holds it can post as the bot, so it's only shown to the bot's creator and to administrators.
class Bot < ApplicationRecord

  belongs_to :user, autosave: true
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validates :name, presence: true

    # Only bots whose user is active can authenticate, so banning a user stops its bots at once. Deactivating a
    # user destroys its bot outright (see User#deactivate).
    def authenticate(code)
      joins(:user).merge(User.active).find_by(code: code) if code.present?

  end

  end

  def avatar=(avatar)

  end

  private

    def bot_user
      user || build_user(password: SecureRandom.hex)
    end
end

# Chat bots Bots are chat members that post messages over HTTP. They're aimed at shell scripts and CI jobs: a deploy script can announce that it finished, a test run can post its summary. ## Model - `Bot` (`bots` table) holds the bot's **code**, the credential that authenticates its requests, and its **creator** (the person who set it up). - Each bot has its own `User` (`bots.user_id`, one-to-one). That user carries the bot's name and avatar and is what messages, memberships and notifications point at. So a bot is an ordinary member as far as the rest of the app is concerned: it's named and avatared like anyone, shows as the author of its messages, joins open rooms when it's created, can be granted closed rooms like anyone, and triggers push notifications the same way. - The bot's user has no email address and a random password nobody knows. Bots never sign in, but the users table requires a password digest. - Deleting a bot (`User#deactivate`, which the bot's delete button and the account members list both use) deactivates its user, the same as for people, and destroys the `Bot` row. That removes the code, so the bot can't post, but its past messages stay attributed to it. Permissions reuse `User#can_administer?(record)`, which already lets a record's creator or an administrator manage it. Any member can create bots. The list shows your own bots, or every bot for administrators. ## Web UI - `/account/edit` has a bot icon link ("Set up chat bots") for every member, not only administrators. - `/bots` lists the bots (no pagination). Each item shows the name, the creator (for administrators), an edit link ("Edit "), and a read-only "Bot code" field with a copy button. The page is marked `turbo-cache-control: no-cache` so Turbo doesn't keep codes in its page cache. - `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` share one form: avatar (optional), name ("Name the bot", required), "Save changes". The edit page adds "Delete this chat bot", which asks for confirmation with Turbo's `data-turbo-confirm` (the native `confirm()`). - Forms that fail validation re-render with status 422. - An empty file field doesn't clear the current avatar. The controller drops blank `avatar` params. ## HTTP API ``` curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \ https://chat.example.com/rooms///messages ``` Route: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` (`bot_messages_path`), handled by `Bots::MessagesController`. | Situation | Status | |---------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------| | Message created | `201 Created`, `Location: /messages/:id` | | Unknown, deleted or banned bot code | `401 Unauthorized` | | Room doesn't exist, or the bot isn't a member of it | `404 Not Found` | | Empty or whitespace-only body and no attachment | `422 Unprocessable Content` | Checks run in that order, so an unknown code gets 401 whatever the room is. messages.content:
Bots are implemented. The full suite passes (358 runs, 0 failures; the 22 skips are existing network/DNS tests), RuboCop is clean and Brakeman reports zero warnings.

I verified the behaviour by driving a running development server with `curl`, using the spec's example. Every documented status code returned as specified, and the bot code was masked in the request log.

**Design**
- A bot is a `Bot` row (the credential, plus its creator) linked one-to-one to a `User`. Messages, memberships, avatars and push notifications all go through that user, so a bot behaves like any other member. Creation joins open rooms, and bots can be granted closed rooms.
- Permissions reuse `User#can_administer?`, which already covers a record's creator and administrators.
- Deleting a bot deactivates its user and destroys the `Bot` row, so the code stops working. Its past messages stay attributed to it.

**Bot API** (`POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages`)
- The raw body is the message. The endpoint skips Rails' form and JSON parsing, because a body like `100% done` otherwise gets a 400. A test confirms this.
- Text is HTML-escaped before storage, so markup in a bot message shows literally.
- Multipart `attachment` uploads work the same way they do in the web app: the file is the message, and any text is ignored.

**Credential handling**
- The code appears in the path, so it's masked in request logs, parameter logs and Sentry URLs.
- The code is shown only on `/bots`, to its creator and to administrators.
- Banning or deactivating a user stops its bots from authenticating.

**UI**: the bot icon link on `/account/edit` (visible to all members), `/bots`, `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit`, with the labels exactly as specified. Confirmation uses Turbo's native `confirm()`.

**Known limits**
- System tests couldn't run here: there's no chromedriver and no network to fetch one. I checked the UI through controller tests and by fetching the rendered pages from the running server. A browser pass is still needed.
- Codes are stored in plaintext, because the list must display them. The app has no encryption keys configured.
- There's no code rotation and no rate limiting on the endpoint.
- Debug-level SQL logs contain literal values, including codes. Session tokens already behave this way, so production should not run at debug level.

Design notes, the API contract and these limits are in `docs/bots.md`.
